humanities_role_explanation: The 19th-century British newspaper texts in the BLN600 dataset serve as raw content (noisy text input). While the material exhibits historical linguistic features (e.g., archaic abbreviations, old currency), the evaluation measures general language modeling denoising capabilities—specifically character-level sequence correction—rather than domain-specific historical analysis or critical interpretation.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: The evaluation uses parallel text sequences consisting of noisy OCR text as inputs and clean, manually transcribed ground-truth text as targets.
analytical_tasks_explanation: The task is post-OCR correction of historical newspapers, focusing on character-level and word-level error repair (including handling substitutions, insertions, deletions, misnamed entities, and extreme OCR corruption/hallucinations).

general_purpose_benchmark.note: The evaluation is strictly scoped to the task of post-OCR correction on a single dataset of historical newspapers (BLN600).

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates Llama 2 (7B and 13B) and compares its performance with BART (Base and Large).

quantitative_metrics.note: Evaluates using percentage reduction in Character Error Rate (CER), computed using Levenshtein distance.

published_after_march_2023.note: Published in May 2024 at the LT4HALA workshop @ LREC-COLING 2024.

summary: This paper evaluates the performance of instruction-tuned generative Large Language Models (specifically Llama 2) against fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence models (BART) for the task of post-OCR correction. Using the BLN600 parallel dataset of 19th-century British newspaper articles, the authors demonstrate that instruction-tuned LLMs can effectively clean noisy OCR text, achieving strong results even under low-data constraints.
key_findings: The instruction-tuned Llama 2 (13B) model achieved a 54.51% reduction in Character Error Rate (CER), significantly outperforming the fine-tuned BART-large model, which achieved a 23.30% reduction. Furthermore, Llama 2 displayed high correction performance with very small training sets, whereas BART's performance deteriorated significantly as the volume of training data decreased.
facets_explanation: The reference answers are retrieved from the pre-existing BLN600 corpus, which features manually re-keyed human transcriptions of 19th-century British Library newspapers, though the paper does not state how these transcribers were trained or selected. Correcting the OCR errors relies on reconstructing the text segment itself, meaning no external knowledge beyond the stimulus is strictly required for the target alignment. The benchmark utilizes a single ground-truth transcription per item to calculate Character Error Rate, and the paper does not address annotator disagreement or alternative transcriptions.
